This is the first phrase.
Regarding the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) to attain the mind of omniscience, one should hold it as precious and not forget it.
These various stages should not be assigned individually; rather, they may be explained collectively.
Alternatively, all these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) belong exclusively to the ten stages (daśabhūmi), for they do not abandon compassion and are all termed "great" (mahat).
They are called "superior intention" (adhyāśaya) because they have already been produced.
If one is still prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), that superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) resides precisely in its own position and is not yet called "cultivated" (*vṛtta*).
For this reason, it is known that [the sūtra] speaks only of the ten stages.
Sūtra: "Bringing sentient beings to fulfillment until the very end, never becoming weary."
The commentary states:
This consists of four points:

first, tirelessness in benefiting sentient beings; second, not abandoning the activities of gathering disciples; third, upholding the true Dharma; and fourth, insatiability in performing virtuous deeds.
Sūtra: "Constantly and joyfully established in [the state] up to being without fear. Commentary:
This consists of five phrases.
First, one should always practice the dedication of whatever wholesome roots one cultivates.
Second, one should seek the Dharma without laziness.
Third, one should expound the Dharma without contraction; "contraction" here refers to shrinking back or withholding.
Because he gives unreservedly, he does not shrink back or cling with stinginess.
Fourth, he provides offerings to all Buddhas with courage.
Fifth, he is fearless regarding birth and death.
The above constitutes ten phrases of the sutra:
"Though encountering rise and fall... one is able to avoid becoming addicted or defiled.
The commentary says:
This consists of five points:
first, being unmoved by the eight winds and neither rejoicing in prosperity nor grieving over decline;
second, not disparaging those of junior learning, for they may surpass oneself in the future.
Third, one has already trained in respectful affection;
fourth, regarding all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) mixed with afflictions (*kleśa*), one is able to reflect according to reality (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and does not allow them to increase;
fifth, one is able to refrain from being attached to or stained by the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Sūtra: Regarding one's own pleasant experiences, one gives rise to the perception of them as being a virtuous friend.
Commentary: This consists of five phrases.
First, not being attached to one's own happiness;
second, not envying the happiness of others;
third, not relishing the various dhyānas.

Fourth, although they traverse the three realms and undergo the four modes of birth to perform transformative guidance, they do so as if wandering through a royal garden, feeling great joy rather than weariness or detachment;
fifth, when they see those who come seeking them, they conceive the thought of them being virtuous friends, for these beings fulfill their great enterprise of attaining bodhi.

This consists of five points:
first, being fond of giving without stinginess;

Third, to rescue and protect those who violate the prohibitions;
fourth, to swiftly fulfill the various perfections (pāramitās) with a gravity like that toward one's parents;

fifth, regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, to act as a worldly attendant and assistant in accomplishing the Noble Path, differing from the two vehicles in that one cultivates them to ultimate perfection.
Sūtra: Regarding all wholesome dharmas, up to the great unimpeded giving.
Commentary: This consists of five phrases.
First, they constantly and diligently cultivate wholesome deeds;
second, they delight in adorning Buddha-fields;
third, they rejoice in praising Buddha-fields.
Fourth, to swiftly attain a Buddha-field; in the older translations, these three were combined into one because they clarify the Buddha-field.
Fifth, to fulfill the primary and secondary marks by practicing unimpeded giving.
This consists of thirty phrases.

This consists of two phrases:
first, adorning the three karmas through the observance of precepts; second, fortifying the body and mind through patience.

Second, one strengthens one's own mind by listening to the Dharma.

For the purpose of bearing [the burden], there is the skillful wisdom of transformation.

First, "thoroughly knowing the three aggregates" refers to the wisdom that enables one to bear the burden of sentient beings; because one possesses this wisdom, one is able to deliver sentient beings. Knowing that only the dharmas can be transformed and delivered, it is called "bearing the burden."
Second is the subduing of Māra through diligence. "Māra" refers to the four māras, and these four constitute the army.
Alternatively, there are ten members of the army, as Nāgārjuna stated:

desire is your first army; sorrow is the second; hunger and thirst are the third army; craving is the fourth; sleep is the fifth army; fear is the sixth; doubt and regret are the seventh army; anger is the eighth; gain and hollow fame are the ninth; and self-exaltation with the disparagement of others is the tenth.
Such hosts as these oppress and submerge those who have left the household life.
By the power of my meditative concentration and wisdom, I shall destroy all your armies, attain the path of Buddhahood, and deliver all people.
Third, being free from pride, one seeks the wisdom of skillful means for transformation;
in order to protect the True Dharma, one does not become conceited, but skillfully seeks the wisdom that benefits others, thereby being able to uphold the Buddha’s True Dharma.

The old translation states: "Constantly seeking the wisdom of the true mark of non-thought. Here, "non-thought" (wunian) refers to untainted right wisdom that is free from all mental recollection; it does not mean the absence of mental activity.

There are three phrases here:
the practitioner, the awakened one, and the one who realizes through silent communion. Although these three flow forth, their wisdom is not ultimate.
They exclusively and profoundly unite with the three [natures], yet they do not abide in those same three as the two vehicles do.
Within this context, although all three objects of focus take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their referent, they do not ultimately realize the unconditioned; this is termed "non-abiding."
Sūtra: "Although they practice non-action, they intentionally take birth.
Commentary: This consists of three phrases.
"Action" (kṛti) refers to volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*), for it is produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Its essence is thus conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); although one practices the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and uncreated (*akṛta*) dharmas, one does not delight in realizing them as a goal.
Although one contemplates that conditioned phenomena will ultimately perish,
one does not weary of the True Suchness of impermanence in performing wholesome deeds.
Although one contemplates the principle of suffering, one intentionally takes birth to bring benefit and happiness to all.
The Mahāyāna principle of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self has already been explained previously in the "Śrāvaka Chapter.
Although one delights in contemplation up to the point of developing revulsion for body and mind, [the text continues: *sūtra*.
The commentary states:
This consists of four propositions.
Observing that there is no self within one's own body, yet not loathing the body, one does not enter nirvana.
Observing that others lack a self-existent sentient being, they transform others without weariness.
Although they contemplate nirvana, they do not ultimately enter eternal extinction, for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

Although one contemplates True Suchness and distances oneself from the body of suffering, one does not grow weary of the body and mind because one has attained peace and happiness; nor does one grow weary of the body and mind because one vows for peace and happiness in order to exhaust birth and death and deliver sentient beings.
Sūtra: Although he delights in observing matters that lead to the ultimate benefit of sentient beings.
Commentary: This consists of two phrases.
Regarding *ālaya*, although it possesses the three collections (*piṭaka*), here we take it in the sense of that which is capable of being the storehouse.
"Without *ālaya*" means there is no entity capable of being the storehouse;
yet, even though the substance of the storehouse is absent, there still exists the phenomenon of being able to store.
This refers to the Mahāyāna teachings of the Dharma-treasury (dharmagarbha).
Among the ten virtues of the sūtra, the eighth is purity and the ninth is brilliant whiteness.
"Purity" means that its intrinsic nature is liberated.

The Dharma he teaches is, even within a single kṣaṇa, free from fault; being devoid of the roots of the three poisons and free from all fetters, it is by nature liberated, for he does not teach while still possessing the three poisons.
"Pure white" (*śukla*) refers to liberation through continuity (*saṃtati-vimukti*).
It is not that there is no fault in a single moment alone; rather, when described in terms of continuity, it is likewise free from all faults.
Furthermore, while the preceding "purity" (*viśuddhi*) refers to the dharma-body being free from faults, this "pure white" enables the bodies of those who train to become pure white as well.

Although they contemplate that birth and death are forever exhausted, they possess no essence that can be grasped or stored, yet they do not abandon the pure and white teachings as they transform sentient beings.
Although they contemplate the principle of non-arising, they constantly carry out the work of bearing burdens to benefit sentient beings.
Sūtra: Although they contemplate the untainted (anāsrava), they do not abandon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Commentary:
This consists of three phrases.
Although one contemplates the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one still accords with the flow of the tainted (*sāsrava*).
"Practice" (*caryā*) has the meaning of movement and activity; non-practice is the unconditioned.
Although one contemplates non-practice, one constantly practices for the benefit and happiness [of others].
Although one contemplates the principle of selflessness both internally and externally, one does not abandon great compassion and thereby uproots the suffering of sentient beings.
[From] the Sūtra: "Although one contemplates non-arising" up to "the wisdom that is cultivated."
The commentary states:
This consists of three phrases.
Although the cause is the same as that of the Two Vehicles in observing the principle of non-arising, one does not follow the formal station of the Two Vehicles.
Although one contemplates emptiness and stillness, one does not render the merit one cultivates empty or still.
Although one contemplates detachment, one does not distance oneself from wisdom.
Sūtra: Although one contemplates all dharmas, one establishes them in the lineage of the Buddhas.
The commentary states:
This consists of three phrases.

Although one contemplates the principle that conditioned phenomena lack substantial reality and the *dharmatā* of *tathatā*, one remains constantly and perfectly established, contemplating without weariness.
Although he contemplates that all phenomena are masterless and are suchness, he seeks spontaneous wisdom with unremitting diligence.
That which possesses signs refers to all conditioned things, just as a king uses a banner as his sign.

Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena possess both characteristics and the characterized; the four characteristics act as the defining marks, while all conditioned phenomena that are characterized serve as that which is marked.
Because this unconditioned state is without such [characteristics], it is called "without signs.
Although one contemplates this unconditioned state, within the teachings of definitive meaning (nītārtha), one hears the true Dharma and establishes the lineage of the Buddha.
Regarding the term "contemplation" mentioned in the above phrases, it refers entirely to the contemplation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the term "not," it refers entirely to non-abiding.
Sūtra: "O sons of good family... up to not abiding in the unconditioned."
The commentary says:
This is the third section. The Sūtra states:
"Furthermore, son of good family... up to... not exhausting the conditioned."
The commentary states:
The third section below uses two pairs of opposites to simultaneously distinguish two types.
There are sixteen pairs; the old translation contains four pairs.
This consists of two pairs.
Those who practice cultivate merit and thus experience superior birth and death;

they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), but cultivate the provisions of wisdom to uproot the suffering of sentient beings and seek great enlightenment, and therefore they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If one abides in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and exhausts the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one becomes a follower of the Two Vehicles and enters eternal quiescence.
This self-benefit at the expense of others is the intended meaning of the following passage.

All should know that if one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and does not enter eternal quiescence like the followers of the two vehicles, one can accomplish the twofold benefit.
Bestowing joy without deficiency, yet not dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
with great compassion benefiting all beings, yet not exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Sūtra: "Benefiting and bringing peace and happiness, up to not exhausting the conditioned."
The commentary states:
Herein there are two pairs.
To benefit sentient beings without ceasing, one does not abide in the unconditioned;
To perfectly accomplish the Buddha-dharma is not to exhaust the conditioned;
to fulfill the Buddha-body is not to abide in the unconditioned;
to attain fearlessness and so forth is not to exhaust the conditioned.
Sūtra: "Skillful means lead to the non-exhaustion of the conditioned.
Commentary: This consists of two pairs.
Skillfully manifesting through transformation, they do not dwell in the unconditioned;
with wondrous wisdom constantly observing, they do not exhaust the conditioned.
Cultivating the perfection of Buddha-lands such as those of retribution and transformation, they do not dwell in the unconditioned.
The Buddha’s reward body (saṃbhogakāya) is eternally abiding and inexhaustible, yet it does not exhaust the conditioned (saṃskṛta).
The Sūtra says: "It constantly performs benefit until the conditioned is exhausted.
The commentary states:
This consists of two pairs:
constantly benefiting sentient beings while not dwelling in the unconditioned;
receiving the Dharma without cessation while not exhausting the conditioned.
The roots of goodness are inexhaustible, yet they do not abide in the unconditioned;
the roots of goodness are indestructible, yet they do not exhaust the conditioned.
By the power of these roots of goodness, the merits sustained by the body are never severed or destroyed, nor are they exhausted within the conditioned.
Sūtra: "In order to fulfill [the path] up to the inexhaustibility of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Commentary: This consists of two pairs.
Having fulfilled their vows to benefit sentient beings, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
they do not aspire to enter forever into ultimate extinction, nor do they exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
With perfectly pure intentions, they advance toward the benefit of others, not abiding in the unconditioned.
The supreme intention is pure and self-benefiting, inexhaustible, yet it does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Sūtra: "He constantly sports until the conditioned is exhausted. Commentary:
This consists of two pairs:
[first,] benefiting sentient beings through the five supernormal powers while not abiding in the unconditioned;
[second,] perfecting Buddha-wisdom and fully completing the six supernormal powers, reaching ultimate inexhaustibility without exhausting the conditioned.
The various perfections fulfill one's own benefit, yet one does not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
because the original intention to benefit others is not yet fulfilled, one does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The *Sūtra* states: "Accumulating the treasures of the Dharma until the conditioned is not exhausted."
The commentary says:
Herein there are two pairs.
Being insatiable regarding the Dharma and wealth, one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
They take no pleasure in the limited teachings of the two vehicles, but manifest only the vast teachings of the Mahāyāna; they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because their vows are never regressive and they constantly deliver sentient beings, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
because their vows are fulfilled without ceasing, they do not exhaust the conditioned.
Sūtra: “Accumulating all conditioned phenomena until they reach inexhaustibility.
Commentary: This consists of two pairs.
One continuously gathers the medicinal herbs of the sublime Dharma without ceasing, yet does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
one administers medicine according to the illness without rest, yet does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because one knows how to apply remedies externally for the illnesses of sentient beings, one does not abide in the unconditioned.
It is able to pacify all illnesses without ever ceasing, never exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Sūtra: “O sons of good family... up to: diligently practicing and studying. Commentary:
This concludes the two [sections on] non-exhaustion and non-abiding.
Scripture: At that time, all those present leaped for joy in body and mind.
Commentary: It says:
From here below is the third section: returning after joyfully making offerings and praising virtues.
It has three parts:
first, rejoicing upon hearing the Dharma; second, making offerings of flowers and incense; and third, praising and prostrating before returning.
This is the first [point].

Having heard the Dharma, those who had not previously attained realization were awakened, and those Bodhisattvas who had already attained realization were encouraged; thus, they rejoiced greatly, their bodies and minds leaping with joy.
[Sutra]: [He] offered incense and flowers as an act of worship, reaching to such an immeasurable depth that they submerged up to his knees. [Commentary]:
This is the offering of flowers and incense.
There are two parts:
first, making offerings to the Three Honored Ones; second, scattering [the offerings] throughout the world.
This may be understood from the text.
Wherever there is the Dharma, it is like a Buddha-stūpa or temple and must necessarily be honored with offerings.

Moreover, it symbolizes that the fundamental nature of the Buddha-land is purely pure, and it also signifies that sentient beings have extinguished their afflictions and evils; therefore, it covers the ground.
It is sufficient for the practice of the Dharma-nature and its benefits, and thus it is deeply submerged up to the knees.
At that time, the various bodhisattvas arrived and proceeded to that land.
Praise says:
Having thus offered praise and prostration, he returned.
He prostrated because he had returned to his physical actions (*kāyakarman*), and he offered praise because he had returned to his verbal actions (*vākkarman*).
Since his beneficial work was complete, he must return to his own kingdom.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Fascicle Six, Part One.
